A concise companion to the book, not a replacement for the full chapters.
The big idea

Java has repeatedly improved the way it manages concurrent work. Virtual threads make it possible to handle many waiting tasks while retaining straightforward, thread-oriented code.

01

Start with the distinction

Java has supported multithreading from the beginning. The chapter traces the journey from manually managed threads through executors and asynchronous APIs to Project Loom.

Concurrency

Dealing with many things

Tasks can make progress over overlapping periods, even if a single core switches between them rather than running them simultaneously.

Parallelism

Doing many things at once

Multiple tasks execute at the same instant, typically on different CPU cores. Parallelism can be a way to implement concurrency.

JAVA 1.0Built-in threads and synchronization
JAVA 5Executors, locks and concurrent collections
JAVA 7–8Fork/Join and CompletableFuture
PROJECT LOOMVirtual threads and structured concurrency
02

Java is made of threads

A thread is an independent path of execution. Threads in a process share memory, while each has its own call stack and execution state. Even a simple main method runs on the main thread; JVM services such as garbage collection also use threads.

Threads give exceptions, debuggers and profilers useful context: a stack trace shows the calls in the thread where an exception occurred, and tools can inspect threads separately.

Creating and starting work

Early Java offered two approaches: extend Thread or implement Runnable. A lambda is a concise way to provide a Runnable, keeping the task separate from the thread. Call start() to begin a new thread; calling run() directly simply runs the task on the current thread.

ThreadDemo.javaJava
public class ThreadDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        System.out.println("Main: " + Thread.currentThread().getName());

        Thread worker = new Thread(() ->
            System.out.println("Worker: " + Thread.currentThread().getName()),
            "worker-1");
        worker.start(); // starts a new thread; run() alone does not
        worker.join();  // wait until the worker has finished
    }
}

Adapted illustration of the chapter’s thread creation examples. Save as ThreadDemo.java, then run javac ThreadDemo.java and java ThreadDemo.

03

The hidden cost of waiting

In the traditional thread-per-request model, a server assigns a platform thread to a request for its lifetime. If that thread blocks while waiting for a database or network response, it remains occupied even though it is not doing useful CPU work.

Memory & limits

Threads have a footprint

Platform threads use native resources, including stack memory. Stack sizes and thread limits depend on the JVM, OS and configuration; creating too many can exhaust resources.

Scheduling

Switching has a cost

Scheduling and context switches consume CPU time. More threads do not automatically mean higher throughput, especially when resources are saturated.

Throughput is completed requests divided by elapsed time. The chapter’s thread-limit experiment is environment-dependent and deliberately exhausts resources; avoid running it on a shared or production machine.
04

Overlap independent work

The chapter’s credit example fetches a person, assets and liabilities, performs other work, and calculates a result. Once the person is known, independent operations can overlap instead of waiting for each other.

Get person→Assets + liabilities + other work→Calculate credit

With five illustrative 200 ms steps, the book reports roughly 1,026 ms sequentially versus 616 ms using separate threads. Those numbers illustrate overlap, not a performance guarantee; actual results depend on dependencies, scheduling and workload. For reliable microbenchmarks, use a tool such as JMH.

Use an executor to manage workers

An ExecutorService separates tasks from thread management. A fixed pool reuses a limited number of platform threads, but tasks may queue and Future.get() still blocks the caller until a result is ready.

PoolDemo.javaJava 19+
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.Future;

public class PoolDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        // try-with-resources for ExecutorService requires Java 19+.
        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2)) {
            Future<Integer> assets = pool.submit(() -> 325_000);
            Future<Integer> debts  = pool.submit(() -> 205_000);
            // get() waits if the result is not ready; it can also report failure.
            System.out.println("Net value: " + (assets.get() - debts.get()));
        } // closes the executor and waits for submitted work
    }
}

A small, runnable adaptation of the chapter’s executor approach. Save as PoolDemo.java. The example needs Java 19+ for executor try-with-resources.

Interruption matters. Prefer propagating InterruptedException when possible. If you catch it and cannot propagate it, restore the interrupt flag before exiting or translating the exception:
Interruption patternJava
try {
    Thread.sleep(200);
} catch (InterruptedException e) {
    Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // restore the interrupted status
    throw new RuntimeException(e);
}

This fragment belongs inside a method; it is not a standalone program.

05

Beyond basic thread pools

A Fork/Join pool uses worker-local queues and work stealing: an idle worker can take work from another worker’s queue. This helps balance suitable workloads, especially tasks that can be divided into smaller pieces. Local queues may improve cache locality, but neither cache affinity nor a speedup is guaranteed.

Related performance concerns include false sharing, where different threads update different variables on the same cache line and trigger costly cache-coherence traffic. This is workload-dependent, not an inevitable property of every pool.

Compose results with CompletableFuture

CompletableFuture adds a fluent API for combining asynchronous stages and handling failures. It can simplify dependencies, but chains require care to understand, debug and manage errors. A final get() or join() still blocks if the result is not ready.

FutureDemo.javaJava 8+
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;

public class FutureDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        CompletableFuture<Integer> assets =
            CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> 325_000);
        CompletableFuture<Integer> debts =
            CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> 205_000);

        CompletableFuture<Integer> net = assets.thenCombine(debts,
            (a, d) -> a - d);
        System.out.println("Net value: " + net.join()); // wait at the boundary
    }
}

Runnable Java 8+ illustration of composition; save as FutureDemo.java. The default asynchronous executor is used here; real blocking I/O needs an appropriate execution strategy.

06

A reactive alternative

Reactive programming models work as asynchronous streams of events and provide operators for transforming and combining them. Frameworks can be a good fit for event-driven streams and complex asynchronous flows, with backpressure used to manage demand where supported.

The trade-off is a different programming model: operators, scheduling and error propagation take time to learn, asynchronous chains can be harder to debug, and framework-specific APIs can increase migration costs. Choose it for a real need, not simply because it is available. Wrapping a blocking call in a reactive type does not automatically make that call non-blocking.

07

The virtual-thread shift

Project Loom introduced lightweight virtual threads, finalized in Java 21. The JVM schedules many virtual threads onto a smaller number of platform threads, allowing applications with many concurrent, waiting tasks to retain a familiar blocking style.

When a virtual thread performs many supported blocking operations, it can unmount from its carrier so that the carrier can run other work. This is not universal: some operations can still occupy a carrier, and pinning behavior depends on the Java version. Virtual threads improve scalability for appropriate workloads; they do not make CPU-bound work faster or remove database, memory or other resource limits.

A thread per task, without a platform-thread pool

The chapter shows that executor-based code can often adopt newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(). Review thread-local state, synchronization, resource limits and library behavior rather than assuming every substitution is safe or faster.

VirtualThreadDemo.javaJava 21+
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.Future;

public class VirtualThreadDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        // Virtual threads are final in Java 21.
        try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            Future<String> result = executor.submit(() -> {
                Thread.sleep(100); // stands in for a blocking operation
                return "Hello from a virtual thread";
            });
            System.out.println(result.get());
        } // closes the executor and waits for submitted work
    }
}

Runnable Java 21+ illustration adapted from the chapter’s virtual-thread executor example. Save as VirtualThreadDemo.java.

ApproachUseful forKeep in mind
Platform thread poolReusing a bounded set of workersBlocked workers and queued tasks can limit throughput.
CompletableFuture / reactiveComposing asynchronous work and streamsExecution flow and errors can be harder to follow.
Virtual threadsMany concurrent tasks that spend time waitingStill subject to CPU, downstream capacity and other limits.
08

Keep these ideas

  • Concurrency is about overlapping work; parallelism is simultaneous execution.
  • Platform threads are valuable but finite. Blocking can tie up expensive resources.
  • Executors manage workers; Fork/Join balances tasks; CompletableFuture composes stages. Each has trade-offs.
  • Virtual threads make thread-per-task designs practical at larger scale for many I/O-heavy workloads, while preserving familiar Java code.
  • Measure and match the model to the problem. More concurrency is not automatically more throughput.

Source: A N M Bazlur Rahman, Modern Concurrency in Java, 1st ed., O’Reilly Media, 2025, Chapter 1, “Introduction,” pp. 1–30 (PDF pages 19–48). Figures 1-1, 1-2 and 1-3 are embedded from the supplied PDF. Copyright © 2025 A N M Bazlur Rahman. The explanations and short code examples above are adapted for study.

Chapter 02 · Understanding virtual threads

Virtual threads make waiting inexpensive enough to support many concurrent tasks—but the application still needs to manage limited resources, cancellation and observability.

01

What is a virtual thread?

A virtual thread is a Thread scheduled by the JVM rather than a one-to-one wrapper around an operating-system thread. The JVM mounts it on a carrier platform thread while it executes. When many supported blocking operations occur, it can unmount and let the carrier run another virtual thread; it can later resume on a different carrier.

Platform thread

OS-scheduled

Typically maps one-to-one to an OS thread. It has a native stack and is relatively expensive to create in large numbers.

Virtual thread

JVM-scheduled

Many virtual threads share a smaller set of carrier platform threads. Their stack data lives in the heap and can grow and shrink.

The JDK’s virtual-thread scheduler uses a dedicated work-stealing ForkJoinPool, separate from the common pool. The OS schedules carriers; it does not directly schedule virtual threads. Carrier count is normally based on available processors and can be configured, but tune only after measurement.

Important: a virtual thread is not a CPU core. It improves the ability to handle many waiting tasks, not the speed of individual CPU-bound calculations.
02

Create, wait & cancel

Virtual threads are final in Java 21. Verify your JDK with java -version; the book also introduces SDKMAN for managing JDK installations.

Start a virtual thread directly, use the builder to name or create it unstarted, or submit tasks to a virtual-thread-per-task executor. Virtual threads are daemon threads, so a program should wait for work to complete instead of relying on them to keep the JVM alive.

VirtualLifecycle.javaJava 21+
public class VirtualLifecycle {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        Thread worker = Thread.ofVirtual().name("hello-worker").unstarted(() ->
            System.out.println("Virtual? " + Thread.currentThread().isVirtual()));
        worker.start();
        worker.join(); // virtual threads are daemon threads: wait for completion

        Thread other = Thread.startVirtualThread(() -> System.out.println("Done"));
        other.join();
    }
}

Runnable Java 21+ example. Save as VirtualLifecycle.java, then run javac VirtualLifecycle.java and java VirtualLifecycle.

Interruption works through the familiar Thread API. It is a cooperative request: code must respond to the interrupt or an interruptible blocking operation. If translating or swallowing InterruptedException, restore the flag where appropriate.

VirtualInterrupt.javaJava 21+
import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;

public class VirtualInterrupt {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        CountDownLatch ready = new CountDownLatch(1);
        Thread worker = Thread.startVirtualThread(() -> {
            try {
                ready.countDown();
                Thread.sleep(10_000);
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // preserve the signal
                System.out.println("Cancelled; cleaning up");
            }
        });
        ready.await();
        worker.interrupt(); // cooperative cancellation, not forced termination
        worker.join();
    }
}

Runnable Java 21+ example; save as VirtualInterrupt.java. Output order can vary.

03

Think in throughput

Virtual threads are especially useful when there are many concurrent tasks and each spends significant time waiting. They can make thread-per-request code practical at higher concurrency without adopting a callback-heavy model.

Little’s Law: for a stable system, average in-flight work N = λ × d, where λ is throughput and d is average time in the system. For example, 100 requests/second at 0.5 seconds average response time corresponds to 50 requests in flight on average. The relationship describes a system; increasing N does not guarantee higher throughput if another resource is saturated.

The chapter compares simulated sleeping tasks on virtual threads and fixed pools. This demonstrates the effect of limited worker concurrency, not a universal benchmark. Measure realistic workloads, include warm-up and repeated runs, and monitor latency and downstream services.

Aggregate independent tasks

Submit independent operations and collect their results with Future.get(). Waiting is still blocking: the waiting thread’s type and operation determine whether a carrier can be released. Handle failures, interruption and timeouts in real services.

PhraseDemo.javaJava 21+
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.Future;

public class PhraseDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            Future<String> adjective = executor.submit(() -> fetch("bright"));
            Future<String> noun = executor.submit(() -> fetch("sunrise"));
            System.out.println(adjective.get() + " " + noun.get());
        } // waits for submitted tasks to finish
    }

    static String fetch(String value) throws InterruptedException {
        Thread.sleep(100); // simulate waiting, not a real network call
        return value;
    }
}

Runnable Java 21+ adaptation of the chapter’s phrase example; save as PhraseDemo.java. main is a platform thread, so its get() calls block that platform thread.

Structured concurrency aims to give related subtasks a shared lifetime and clearer failure and cancellation handling. Its API has been a preview feature and varies by JDK release; check your JDK’s documentation and preview requirements before using it.

04

Protect scarce resources

Cheap threads do not make database connections, API quotas or memory unlimited. Prefer a virtual thread per task rather than pooling virtual threads merely to restrict concurrency; use explicit limits around the scarce resource instead.

A Semaphore caps how many tasks access a resource at once. Acquire before entering the protected operation and release exactly once in finally after successful acquisition. A timeout keeps tasks from waiting forever.

ResourceLimitDemo.javaJava 21+
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;

public class ResourceLimitDemo {
    private static final Semaphore permits = new Semaphore(2);

    static void useResource(int id) throws InterruptedException {
        if (!permits.tryAcquire(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {
            System.out.println("Timed out: " + id);
            return; // nothing acquired, so nothing to release
        }
        try {
            System.out.println("Using resource: " + id);
            Thread.sleep(100); // stand-in for a limited external resource
        } finally {
            permits.release(); // exactly once, even if interrupted
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            var tasks = new java.util.ArrayList<java.util.concurrent.Future<?>>();
            for (int i = 0; i < 6; i++) {
                final int id = i;
                tasks.add(executor.submit(() -> { useResource(id); return null; }));
            }
            for (var task : tasks) task.get(); // surface task failures
        }
    }
}

Runnable Java 21+ example; save as ResourceLimitDemo.java. At most two tasks are inside the protected section at a time.

Concurrency limit ≠ rate limit. A semaphore alone limits simultaneous operations, not requests per second. Time-based quotas require a separate rate-limiting mechanism.
05

Understand pinning

A pinned virtual thread cannot unmount from its carrier while blocked. Frequent or long pinning can tie up carriers and reduce scalability; a short critical section is usually less concerning than one that blocks for a long time.

SituationWhat to know
JDK 21–23Blocking inside synchronized can pin a carrier. For frequent long blocking operations, consider a suitable ReentrantLock and always unlock in finally.
JDK 24+JEP 491 removes nearly all monitor-related pinning. Do not replace every synchronized block blindly; locks still serialize access.
Native / foreign codeNative interactions can still cause pinning or occupy a carrier. Check your JDK and libraries, and measure actual behavior.

Carrier names printed before and after an operation are not reliable proof of pinning: a virtual thread can happen to resume on the same carrier even when it was unmounted. Use diagnostic events instead.

06

Revisit ThreadLocal

ThreadLocal remains supported, but each virtual thread can have its own value. Large per-thread objects that were tolerable in a small platform-thread pool may become costly across many virtual threads. InheritableThreadLocal values, unlike ordinary ThreadLocal values, can be inherited by child threads.

These JConsole screenshots illustrate the book’s specific experiment, not a universal memory ratio. Object lifetime, allocation, garbage collection and workload all affect results. Keep context small, remove values when appropriate, and avoid using thread-local variables to pool expensive resources.

ThreadLocal patternJava fragment
// Fragment: per-thread request context, kept small and cleaned up.
private static final ThreadLocal<String> REQUEST_ID = new ThreadLocal<>();

static void handleRequest(String id) {
    REQUEST_ID.set(id);
    try {
        processRequest();
    } finally {
        REQUEST_ID.remove();
    }
}

Illustrative fragment; processRequest() represents application code. Scoped values are another option for bounded, read-only bindings; their availability and preview status depend on your JDK.

07

Observe the behavior

Java Flight Recorder (JFR) can capture virtual-thread events, including jdk.VirtualThreadPinned and jdk.VirtualThreadSubmitFailed. Start and end events can be enabled when lifecycle detail is needed. Event settings and thresholds depend on the JDK and recording configuration.

Use jcmd virtual-thread-aware dumps to examine tasks, and correlate them with CPU, heap, GC, latency, throughput and downstream saturation. The newer dump format does not contain all information from a traditional thread dump.

Diagnostic commandsShell
# Replace <PID> with the running Java process ID.
jcmd <PID> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json threads.json

# JDK 21–23: print stack traces for blocking while pinned.
java -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full MyApp

# Trace ThreadLocal values set by virtual threads.
java -Djdk.traceVirtualThreadLocals=true MyApp

Replace MyApp and <PID> with your program and process ID. The legacy pinning trace property is specific to older JDKs and has no effect in JDK 24+; use JFR and your JDK’s current diagnostics instead. The ThreadLocal flag traces setting values, not every read.

08

Migration checklist

  • Start with waiting-heavy work and benchmark against your current implementation.
  • Bound downstream access using connection pools, semaphores or rate limits suited to the resource.
  • Review pinning for your JDK version and update libraries where needed.
  • Audit ThreadLocal usage, memory, task lifetimes, cancellation and error handling.
  • Monitor real outcomes: throughput, latency, CPU, heap, GC, JFR events and dependent services.

Source: A N M Bazlur Rahman, Modern Concurrency in Java, 1st ed., O’Reilly Media, 2025, Chapter 2, “Understanding Virtual Threads,” pp. 31–89 (PDF pages 49–107). Figures 2-1 through 2-5 are embedded from the supplied PDF. Copyright © 2025 A N M Bazlur Rahman. The explanations and short code examples are adapted for study.

Chapter 03 · The mechanics of modern concurrency in Java

To understand virtual threads, look beneath their familiar API: workers and queues schedule tasks, while continuations preserve execution state across a pause and resume.

01

Workers, queues & lifecycle

A thread pool reuses a set of worker threads to execute submitted tasks. Workers take tasks from a queue, run them, and then take more work; when all workers are busy, additional tasks may have to wait. Pool designs differ in how workers are created, how tasks are queued, and what happens under overload.

Submit a task→Queue if needed→Worker executes→Worker reused

Reusing platform threads can reduce creation overhead and cap the number of active workers. A bounded queue can limit queued work; an unbounded queue can grow until memory or latency becomes a problem. A worker limit is not automatically a time-based rate limit.

About the book’s homemade pool: it is a teaching sketch, not a production implementation. An empty queue does not mean tasks already taken by workers have finished, and interrupts or task failures require careful handling. Prefer the JDK’s executors for real applications.
02

Configure the executor

ThreadPoolExecutor combines a core and maximum worker count, idle timeout, work queue, thread factory and rejection policy. Normally it creates workers up to the core size, then queues work; if the queue is full it can grow up to the maximum, then rejects according to its policy. Shut it down when no longer needed.

ExecutorBehavior / trade-off
FixedReuses a fixed number of platform workers; newFixedThreadPool uses an unbounded queue.
CachedReuses idle workers and may create many threads when demand rises; it is not a bounded concurrency limit.
Single-threadedExecutes tasks sequentially, useful when work must not overlap.
ScheduledRuns delayed or periodic tasks; periodic tasks need explicit lifecycle management.
Work-stealingUses a Fork/Join pool to distribute tasks; execution order is not guaranteed.

The example below explicitly bounds both workers and the queue. AbortPolicy throws RejectedExecutionException when saturated or shut down; production callers must decide how to handle rejection.

BoundedPoolDemo.javaJava 21+
import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.Future;
import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;

public class BoundedPoolDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        try (var pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
                2, 2, 0L, TimeUnit.SECONDS,
                new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(4),
                new ThreadPoolExecutor.AbortPolicy())) {
            Future<Integer> result = pool.submit(() -> 6 * 7);
            System.out.println("Result: " + result.get());
        } // shuts down the executor and waits for submitted work
    }
}

Runnable Java 21+ adaptation; save as BoundedPoolDemo.java, then run javac BoundedPoolDemo.java and java BoundedPoolDemo.

Callable and Future

A Callable<V> returns a value and may throw an exception; submitting it gives a Future<V>. get() waits for the result and reports task failures through ExecutionException. A timed get can time out, and cancel(true) requests interruption rather than forcibly stopping arbitrary code.

FutureResultDemo.javaJava 21+
import java.util.concurrent.Callable;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.Future;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException;

public class FutureResultDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        try (var pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2)) {
            Callable<Long> task = () -> 21L * 2;
            Future<Long> result = pool.submit(task);
            try {
                System.out.println("Result: " + result.get(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS));
            } catch (TimeoutException e) {
                result.cancel(true); // request interruption if still running
                System.out.println("Timed out");
            }
        }
    }
}

Runnable Java 21+ example; save as FutureResultDemo.java. Closing an executor waits for work to terminate, so cancellation is not a guaranteed hard deadline.

03

Fork, join & steal

Recursive tasks submitted to a fixed pool can suffer thread-starvation deadlock: every worker waits for child tasks that are still queued, leaving no worker free to run them. The chapter illustrates this with recursive Fibonacci work.

For suitable divide-and-conquer work, ForkJoinPool uses worker-local deques and work stealing. A worker can fork one subtask, compute another, and join the result; the pool can help execute relevant tasks while waiting. This is not a guarantee against every deadlock or arbitrary blocking operation.

In the default recursive mode, workers commonly process local tasks in LIFO order while idle workers steal older work from the other end. Async mode favors FIFO local scheduling for event-style tasks; it does not guarantee a global submission or completion order. Virtual threads use a separate Fork/Join-based scheduler in async mode.

FibonacciForkJoin.javaJava 21+
import java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool;
import java.util.concurrent.RecursiveTask;

public class FibonacciForkJoin {
    static final class Fib extends RecursiveTask<Long> {
        private final int n;
        Fib(int n) { this.n = n; }

        protected Long compute() {
            if (n <= 1) return (long) n;
            if (n <= 10) return sequential(n); // avoid tiny tasks
            Fib left = new Fib(n - 1);
            left.fork();
            long right = new Fib(n - 2).compute();
            return right + left.join();
        }
    }

    static long sequential(int n) {
        if (n <= 1) return n;
        return sequential(n - 1) + sequential(n - 2);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (var pool = new ForkJoinPool()) {
            System.out.println("F(20) = " + pool.invoke(new Fib(20)));
        }
    }
}

Runnable Java 21+ example; save as FibonacciForkJoin.java. Expected result: F(20) = 6765. Fibonacci is illustrative; this recursive algorithm repeats work and is not a good performance benchmark.

04

Compare, set, retry

Compare-and-set (CAS) atomically changes a value only if it still matches an expected value. If another thread changed it first, the operation fails and the caller can retry. Fork/Join uses atomic operations as part of its concurrent queue implementation; details are JVM-specific.

CasCounter.javaJava 9+
import java.lang.invoke.MethodHandles;
import java.lang.invoke.VarHandle;

public class CasCounter {
    private volatile int value;
    private static final VarHandle VALUE;
    static {
        try {
            VALUE = MethodHandles.lookup()
                .findVarHandle(CasCounter.class, "value", int.class);
        } catch (ReflectiveOperationException e) {
            throw new ExceptionInInitializerError(e);
        }
    }
    void increment() {
        int current;
        do {
            current = value;
        } while (!VALUE.compareAndSet(this, current, current + 1));
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        CasCounter counter = new CasCounter();
        Runnable work = () -> {
            for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) counter.increment();
        };
        Thread a = new Thread(work);
        Thread b = new Thread(work);
        a.start(); b.start();
        a.join(); b.join(); // wait for both increments to finish
        System.out.println("Counter: " + counter.value); // 200
    }
}

Runnable Java 9+ adaptation of the chapter’s VarHandle counter; save as CasCounter.java. Joining both threads makes the final result deterministic. For ordinary counters, prefer simpler utilities such as AtomicInteger when suitable.

CAS avoids a conventional lock in this counter, but retries can become expensive under contention. It is not automatically faster than a lock for every workload.

05

Pause & resume

A continuation represents suspended execution that can later resume at its previous point. Virtual-thread implementations use continuations to preserve execution state: on a supported blocking operation, the virtual thread can unmount and the carrier becomes available; later, the virtual thread is scheduled to resume.

The book explains heap-backed stack chunks and lazy restoration of frames, using return barriers to avoid restoring an entire stack eagerly. These diagrams describe a conceptual implementation, not a public Java contract; JVM details can change.

Internal API warning: jdk.internal.vm.Continuation is not a supported public API. The following is a learning experiment modeled on the chapter, not production code; it requires exports at compile and run time and may break or be unavailable on other JDK versions.
ContinuationDemo.javaInternal API · experimental
import jdk.internal.vm.Continuation;
import jdk.internal.vm.ContinuationScope;

public class ContinuationDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var scope = new ContinuationScope("demo");
        var continuation = new Continuation(scope, () -> {
            System.out.println("Before yield");
            Continuation.yield(scope);
            System.out.println("After yield");
        });
        continuation.run(); // prints before yield, then returns to main
        System.out.println("Back in main");
        continuation.run(); // resumes after the yield
    }
}
Compile & runShell
# Educational experiment only: internal API; check compatibility with your JDK version.
javac --add-exports java.base/jdk.internal.vm=ALL-UNNAMED ContinuationDemo.java
java --add-exports java.base/jdk.internal.vm=ALL-UNNAMED ContinuationDemo

Save as ContinuationDemo.java. If your JDK exposes these internals with the same API, it prints “Before yield”, “Back in main”, then “After yield”. Use public virtual-thread APIs in applications.

06

From NanoThread to I/O

The book’s NanoThread is a simplified teaching model: a continuation wraps a task, a scheduler runs it on Fork/Join workers, and a timer simulates an I/O completion that reschedules it after yielding. A resumed task may run on a different worker. The sketch is not a production scheduler: safe coordination of yield and rescheduling, lifecycle, failures and cleanup are nontrivial.

In actual JDK networking, a virtual thread waiting on supported socket operations can park and later be unparked when a platform-specific poller reports readiness. The scheduler can then resume it on a carrier. Exact implementation and platform mechanisms vary; not all blocking operations release a carrier, and native calls or pinning can still tie one up.

07

Keep these ideas

  • Pool workers and queue capacity solve different problems. Plan for saturation, rejection and shutdown.
  • Callable and Future separate submission from result collection. Waiting, failure, timeout and cancellation still need attention.
  • Fork/Join works well for suitable decomposable tasks. Local deques and stealing distribute work; arbitrary blocking is still risky.
  • CAS performs an atomic conditional update. A retry loop can contend and is not universally faster than locking.
  • Continuations preserve state across suspension. The JVM combines them with scheduling and I/O readiness to make many waiting virtual threads practical.

Source: A N M Bazlur Rahman, Modern Concurrency in Java, 1st ed., O’Reilly Media, 2025, Chapter 3, “The Mechanics of Modern Concurrency in Java,” pp. 91–123 (PDF pages 109–141). Figures 3-1 through 3-7 are embedded from the supplied PDF. Copyright © 2025 A N M Bazlur Rahman. The explanations and short code examples are adapted for study.

Chapter 04 · Structured concurrency

When one task creates several related subtasks, treat them as one operation: define their lifetime, joining policy, failure behavior and cancellation together.

01

Why structure concurrent work?

Imagine fetching a product and its reviews concurrently. With an executor and separate futures, the relationship between these tasks is not built into the API. A failure, timeout or interruption may require explicit sibling cancellation and cleanup; otherwise, work whose result is no longer needed can continue.

Structured concurrency gives related subtasks a lexical scope. The owner forks them, waits for a chosen outcome and closes the scope before continuing. Task relationships become easier to reason about and inspect.

Version note: this chapter and its examples use the JDK 25 preview version of StructuredTaskScope (JEP 505). Enable preview features at compilation and runtime. The API differs from earlier previews and may change in later JDKs; use the documentation for your exact release.
02

Open, fork, join, close

Open scope→Fork subtasks→Join outcome→Close scope

By default, StructuredTaskScope.open() starts subtasks on virtual threads and requires all of them to succeed. If one fails, the scope interrupts unfinished siblings and join() throws a FailedException with the original failure as its cause. Once joined successfully, retrieve each successful subtask’s result.

The owner thread opens the scope, forks subtasks, calls join() once, and closes it. After joining, it cannot fork more tasks. Use try-with-resources so the scope closes reliably. Closing waits for the threads it started to finish, including interrupted tasks.

StructuredProductDemo.javaJDK 25 preview
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.StructuredTaskScope;

public class StructuredProductDemo {
    record Product(String name) {}
    record ProductInfo(Product product, List<String> reviews) {}

    static ProductInfo fetchProductInfo(boolean fail) throws InterruptedException {
        try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open()) {
            var product = scope.fork(() -> {
                if (fail) throw new IllegalStateException("Product unavailable");
                Thread.sleep(100); // simulate waiting for a service
                return new Product("Java book");
            });
            var reviews = scope.fork(() -> {
                Thread.sleep(200);
                return List.of("Helpful", "Clear");
            });
            scope.join(); // all succeed, or failure cancels remaining work
            return new ProductInfo(product.get(), reviews.get());
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        System.out.println(fetchProductInfo(false));
        try {
            fetchProductInfo(true);
        } catch (StructuredTaskScope.FailedException e) {
            System.out.println("Failed: " + e.getCause().getMessage());
        }
    }
}
Compile & runShell
# Use JDK 25 for the chapter's preview API.
javac --release 25 --enable-preview StructuredProductDemo.java
java --enable-preview StructuredProductDemo

Complete example adapted from the chapter; save as StructuredProductDemo.java. The simulated requests sleep rather than contact real services. The second invocation illustrates failure handling.

03

Choose a joining policy

A Joiner determines when the scope can finish waiting and what join() returns. Select a policy that matches the operation rather than assuming every failure should cancel every sibling.

JDK 25 policyOutcomeTypical use
awaitAllSuccessfulOrThrow()Waits for all to succeed; fails on a subtask failure. Returns null.Default; results may have different types.
allSuccessfulOrThrow()All succeed or the scope fails; returns a stream of subtasks in fork order.Collect results of the same type.
anySuccessfulResultOrThrow()Returns a successful result and cancels remaining work; fails if all fail.Race equivalent replicas.
awaitAll()Waits for all regardless of individual failures and returns null.Inspect each subtask or collect partial outcomes.
allUntil(predicate)Returns a stream of subtasks; the predicate can trigger early cancellation.Custom stop condition; some results may be unavailable.

Race for a successful result

FirstSuccessDemo.javaJDK 25 preview
import java.util.concurrent.StructuredTaskScope;

public class FirstSuccessDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        var joiner = StructuredTaskScope.Joiner.<String>anySuccessfulResultOrThrow();
        try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open(joiner)) {
            scope.fork(() -> { Thread.sleep(100); return "Replica A"; });
            scope.fork(() -> { Thread.sleep(200); return "Replica B"; });
            System.out.println("First success: " + scope.join());
        } // remaining tasks are interrupted and awaited on close
    }
}

Complete JDK 25 preview example; save as FirstSuccessDemo.java and compile/run using the same commands above with this class name. Scheduling is nondeterministic, so do not rely on a particular winner.

Collect partial outcomes

PartialResultsDemo.javaJDK 25 preview
import java.util.concurrent.StructuredTaskScope;

public class PartialResultsDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        var joiner = StructuredTaskScope.Joiner.<String>awaitAll();
        try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open(joiner)) {
            var email = scope.fork(() -> "Email delivered");
            var sms = scope.fork(() -> {
                return failSms();
            });
            scope.join(); // wait for both, regardless of individual failure
            report("Email", email);
            report("SMS", sms);
        }
    }

    static String failSms() { throw new IllegalStateException("SMS failed"); }

    static void report(String label, StructuredTaskScope.Subtask<String> task) {
        switch (task.state()) {
            case SUCCESS -> System.out.println(label + ": " + task.get());
            case FAILED -> System.out.println(label + ": " + task.exception());
            case UNAVAILABLE -> System.out.println(label + ": unavailable");
        }
    }
}

Complete JDK 25 preview example; save as PartialResultsDemo.java. The joiner itself returns null; the retained handles are inspected after joining.

04

Failure is a policy decision

With a fail-fast joiner, inspect FailedException.getCause() to map a domain error or propagate it to a layer with more context. For optional data, a subtask may instead handle a known error and return an explicit fallback. With awaitAll(), inspect individual subtask states rather than assuming they all succeeded.

Cancellation is cooperative. Interrupting a subtask does not forcibly terminate it or undo its external side effects. A task that ignores interruption or blocks in an uninterruptible operation can delay scope closure indefinitely. Design cleanup, timeouts, idempotency and compensation separately.

Propagate InterruptedException where possible; if translating it, restore the interrupted status. Structured concurrency does not make a multi-service operation transactional.

05

Configure the scope

In the JDK 25 API, configuration can provide a name for diagnostics, a thread factory and a timeout. The default creates unnamed virtual threads and has no timeout. A custom factory can create named virtual or platform threads; platform-thread resource limits still apply.

ScopeTimeoutDemo.javaJDK 25 preview
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.concurrent.StructuredTaskScope;

public class ScopeTimeoutDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        var joiner = StructuredTaskScope.Joiner.<String>allSuccessfulOrThrow();
        try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open(joiner,
                config -> config.withName("product-lookup")
                                .withTimeout(Duration.ofMillis(100)))) {
            scope.fork(() -> { Thread.sleep(1_000); return "slow result"; });
            scope.join();
        } catch (StructuredTaskScope.TimeoutException e) {
            System.out.println("Scope timed out");
        }
    }
}

Complete JDK 25 preview example; save as ScopeTimeoutDemo.java. Compile and run with preview enabled as above. The timeout starts when the scope opens; expiration cancels the scope and join() throws StructuredTaskScope.TimeoutException.

A timeout bounds the wait for the join outcome, not necessarily the time to exit the try block: close() still waits for started subtasks to finish.

06

When built-ins aren’t enough

The chapter explores custom joiners for collecting successes and failures, quorum-style completion, and early stopping after too many failures. A JDK 25 Joiner has a result() method and optional onFork() / onComplete() hooks; a hook can request cancellation. Completion callbacks can run concurrently, so implementations must be thread-safe. Create a fresh joiner for each scope.

Prefer built-in policies when they fit, keep custom policy separate from business logic, and test early cancellation and races. Cancellation can prevent later forks from starting. A semaphore can limit concurrent resource use, but it is not a time-based request rate limiter; permit accounting and interruption need particular care.

07

Nested scopes & visibility

A subtask can open another scope to decompose its work into smaller operations. This creates a task tree; each scope joins and closes within its own lexical lifetime. A nested failure affects its parent when it is propagated out of that subtask, subject to the parent’s chosen policy. Nested scopes should close in reverse order of opening.

Actions by the owner before forking happen-before the subtask’s actions; those actions happen-before the successful subtask result is retrieved. This visibility guarantee does not make concurrent mutations of shared objects safe. Use appropriate synchronization, atomic variables or concurrent collections when multiple subtasks update the same state, and do not assume an early join means every canceled task has finished.

08

See the task hierarchy

Named scopes and threads make it easier to understand concurrent work in thread dumps. The chapter shows a virtual-thread-aware jcmd JSON dump with scope containers and their owners. Capture it while the scope is active; a scope already closed may no longer appear.

Thread dumpShell
# Replace <PID> with the process ID while the application is still running.
jcmd <PID> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json threads.json

Run with a compatible JDK and a running Java process. Programmatic dumps are also available through HotSpotDiagnosticMXBean; avoid exposing sensitive thread information unnecessarily.

09

Keep these ideas

  • Group related subtasks into one scope so the task hierarchy and lifetime are explicit.
  • Choose a joiner deliberately: all-success, first-success and partial-result policies handle failures differently.
  • Cancellation requests interruption; it does not force termination. Close waits for started subtasks.
  • Configure timeouts and names, while protecting scarce external resources independently.
  • Use the correct JDK preview API. Structured concurrency is version-sensitive; test against the JDK you deploy.

Source: A N M Bazlur Rahman, Modern Concurrency in Java, 1st ed., O’Reilly Media, 2025, Chapter 4, “Structured Concurrency,” pp. 125–215 (PDF pages 143–233). Figures 4-1 through 4-3 are embedded from the supplied PDF. Copyright © 2025 A N M Bazlur Rahman. Explanations and code examples are adapted for study.

Chapter 05 · Scoped values

ScopedValue carries context through a bounded execution flow without adding it to every intermediate method signature. It is final in JDK 25.

01

The cost of passing context

The chapter’s job scheduler creates a JobContext containing a job name, priority and metadata. If framework callbacks and helper methods must pass it through layers that do not use it, signatures become noisy and user code can become coupled to framework details.

Explicit arguments are still a good default: they make dependencies visible and are often easier to test. Scoped values are useful when a framework needs to carry read-mostly context through a deep call chain without exposing it in every intermediate signature.

Scheduler creates context→Job calls helpers→Framework reads context
02

What ThreadLocal solves—and costs

ThreadLocal keeps a separate value per thread and lets code access context without an explicit parameter. Its values are mutable through set(), and in reused worker threads an unset or forgotten remove() can retain data or leak it into a later task. Cleanup belongs in finally; nested uses may need to restore a previous value rather than simply remove it.

ThreadLocalCleanupDemo.javaJDK 21+
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;

public class ThreadLocalCleanupDemo {
    private static final ThreadLocal<String> USER = new ThreadLocal<>();

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        try (var pool = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor()) {
            pool.submit(() -> {
                USER.set("Alice");
                try {
                    System.out.println("First task: " + USER.get());
                } finally {
                    USER.remove(); // do not leak context to the next task
                }
            }).get();
            System.out.println("Next task: " + pool.submit(USER::get).get());
        }
    }
}

Runnable JDK 21+ example; save as ThreadLocalCleanupDemo.java. Waiting on the first future makes the ordering explicit; the next task prints null.

InheritableThreadLocal can propagate values to newly created child threads, but inheritance adds per-thread bookkeeping and can retain references. By default it copies the reference, not a deep copy of the referenced object; custom inheritance logic can behave differently. With many virtual threads, even modest per-thread state may add up.

03

Bind a scoped value

Create a key with ScopedValue.newInstance(), then bind it for a dynamic execution scope using ScopedValue.where(key, value).run(...). Code called directly or indirectly inside that operation can read the binding with get(). When the call returns or throws, the prior binding is automatically restored or the key becomes unbound.

Bound lifetime

Dynamic scope

The binding follows the execution of the scoped operation and its calls, rather than existing until manually removed.

Read-only binding

Value reference

The binding cannot be changed in place; a nested operation may rebind it. The referenced object itself can still be mutable.

Use call() when the scoped operation must return a result. isBound() tests for a binding; an unbound get() throws NoSuchElementException. orElse() supplies a fallback and orElseThrow() provides a custom exception when unbound. A key can be bound to null, which is distinct from being unbound.

ScopedJobDemo.javaJDK 25
public class ScopedJobDemo {
    record JobContext(String name, String priority) {}
    private static final ScopedValue<JobContext> CONTEXT = ScopedValue.newInstance();

    static void schedule(Runnable job, String name, String priority) {
        var context = new JobContext(name, priority);
        ScopedValue.where(CONTEXT, context).run(job);
    }

    static void frameworkLog() {
        var context = CONTEXT.get();
        System.out.println(context.name() + " / " + context.priority());
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        schedule(ScopedJobDemo::frameworkLog, "backup", "HIGH");
        System.out.println("Bound afterward? " + CONTEXT.isBound());
    }
}
Compile & runShell
# JDK 25: ScopedValue is a stable API; no preview flag is needed here.
javac --release 25 ScopedJobDemo.java
java ScopedJobDemo

Runnable JDK 25 example adapted from the book’s job scheduler. No preview flag is needed for ScopedValue itself in JDK 25.

Access is a capability. Keep the key private where appropriate and expose only necessary operations. This supports encapsulation but does not make mutable objects thread-safe or replace an authorization design.
04

Nested bindings & return values

Bindings can be chained for multiple keys. A nested where() can temporarily rebind a key; when the inner operation ends, the outer value returns automatically, including on exceptional exit. The book illustrates this with roles, graphics settings and recursion depth.

ScopedBindingDemo.javaJDK 25
public class ScopedBindingDemo {
    private static final ScopedValue<String> ROLE = ScopedValue.newInstance();
    private static final ScopedValue<String> REQUEST = ScopedValue.newInstance();

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Outside: " + ROLE.orElse("guest"));
        String result = ScopedValue.where(ROLE, "admin")
            .where(REQUEST, "req-42")
            .call(() -> {
                System.out.println("Outer: " + ROLE.get());
                ScopedValue.where(ROLE, "reader").run(() ->
                    System.out.println("Inner: " + ROLE.get()));
                System.out.println("Restored: " + ROLE.get());
                return REQUEST.get() + " / " + ROLE.get();
            });
        System.out.println("Result: " + result);
        System.out.println("Bound afterward? " + ROLE.isBound());
    }
}

Runnable JDK 25 example; save as ScopedBindingDemo.java and compile/run as above using this class name. It demonstrates call(), multiple keys and restoration after a nested binding.

05

Context across threads

A newly started platform or virtual thread does not automatically inherit scoped-value bindings just because it was started inside a binding. Bind the context in that thread or pass it explicitly. With structured concurrency, subtasks inherit the bindings captured when their StructuredTaskScope is opened; bindings must match when forking.

ScopedInheritanceDemo.javaJDK 25 preview
import java.util.concurrent.StructuredTaskScope;

public class ScopedInheritanceDemo {
    private static final ScopedValue<String> REQUEST = ScopedValue.newInstance();

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        String result = ScopedValue.where(REQUEST, "req-42").call(() -> {
            Thread independent = Thread.startVirtualThread(() ->
                System.out.println("Ordinary child bound? " + REQUEST.isBound()));
            independent.join();

            // Open the task scope while the request binding is in effect.
            try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open()) {
                var first = scope.fork(() -> REQUEST.get() + " / product");
                var second = scope.fork(() -> REQUEST.get() + " / reviews");
                scope.join();
                return first.get() + ", " + second.get();
            }
        });
        System.out.println(result);
    }
}
Compile & runShell
# JDK 25: StructuredTaskScope is still a preview API.
javac --release 25 --enable-preview ScopedInheritanceDemo.java
java --enable-preview ScopedInheritanceDemo

Runnable example for JDK 25. ScopedValue is stable, but StructuredTaskScope is a JDK 25 preview feature and requires preview flags. The output shows an ordinary child is unbound and both structured subtasks can read the request ID.

The structured scope closes before the enclosing binding ends and waits for its started subtasks. Cancellation remains cooperative; it does not forcibly stop tasks or guarantee immediate garbage collection.

06

Choose the right context tool

ApproachGood fitConsiderations
Explicit parametersClear, local dependencies and straightforward tests.Can add pass-through parameters across deep framework layers.
ThreadLocalMutable per-thread state or existing library integrations.Manage cleanup, nesting, thread reuse and per-thread memory.
ScopedValueRead-mostly context with a bounded dynamic lifetime.Not a drop-in replacement for mutable state or arbitrary asynchronous propagation.

Start with request IDs, immutable configuration or other downward-flowing context. Audit library compatibility, nested binding and unbound behavior; prefer immutable data when sharing among subtasks. A scoped value can carry a transaction identifier, but it does not create a transaction, guarantee rollback or make a database connection safe to share.

The book discusses memory and performance benefits, particularly with many virtual threads. These depend on the workload and runtime: measure allocation, latency and throughput rather than assuming a universal speedup. ScopedValue is final in JDK 25; earlier JDKs offered different preview versions, so check their exact APIs and flags before migrating.

07

Keep these ideas

  • Use scoped values for bounded, downward-flowing context when explicit parameters are impractical.
  • Bindings are fixed, but objects may be mutable. Protect shared state and prefer immutable values.
  • Nested rebinding restores the outer binding automatically; unbound get() throws.
  • Ordinary child threads do not inherit bindings automatically; structured subtasks inherit the scope’s captured bindings.
  • Evaluate migration case by case and measure real workloads; JDK 25 finalized ScopedValue.

Source: A N M Bazlur Rahman, Modern Concurrency in Java, 1st ed., O’Reilly Media, 2025, Chapter 5, “Scoped Values,” pp. 217–245 (PDF pages 235–263). The chapter contains no numbered figures; the two study diagrams above are original illustrations. Explanations and code examples are adapted for study.

Chapter 06 · Reactive Java & virtual threads

Virtual threads make blocking-style concurrency more scalable, but reactive streams remain useful for composing ongoing event flows and managing demand.

01

Blocking, non-blocking & I/O

The chapter contrasts a single-threaded blocking server, a platform-thread pool, virtual threads and non-blocking NIO. A blocking call waits for a result; with a platform thread, that thread remains occupied. With a virtual thread, many supported blocking operations can release the carrier while waiting.

With a non-blocking selectable channel, a read or write may make partial progress—or no progress—without waiting for all data. A Selector can wait for readiness across multiple channels, allowing an event loop to handle connections with a small number of threads. Readiness is not the same as completion: an operation may still transfer fewer bytes than requested.

NIO is not automatically non-blocking. Selectable network channels must be configured as non-blocking; FileChannel operations are not selector-based non-blocking operations. Direct buffers do not automatically guarantee zero-copy transfers.

Network protocols need careful per-connection state, incremental parsing and partial-write handling. This fragment retains the buffer position across readiness notifications:

Partial NIO writeJava fragment
// Fragment: keep the SAME ByteBuffer until every byte has been written.
// This method is called when the non-blocking SocketChannel is writable.
static boolean flush(SocketChannel channel, ByteBuffer pending) throws IOException {
    channel.write(pending);       // may write only some bytes, or zero
    return !pending.hasRemaining(); // false: retain buffer and retry on OP_WRITE
}

Illustrative fragment, not a complete server. It needs java.io.IOException, java.nio.ByteBuffer and java.nio.channels.SocketChannel imports.

The book’s HTTP examples are educational sketches, not production-ready protocol implementations. Real servers must preserve HTTP/1.1 pipelined response order, correctly frame bodies in bytes, handle partial reads/writes, bound resources and support timeouts; use a maintained HTTP server for production.

02

The event-loop model

Event-driven frameworks such as Vert.x and Netty run short handlers in response to readiness, timers or messages. A timer schedules a later callback; unlike sleeping in the handler, it leaves the event loop free to process other events.

Blocking or lengthy CPU work in an event-loop callback delays other events on that loop. Offload unavoidable blocking work to an appropriate worker executor using the framework’s APIs, and bound the resources used. Offloading is a valid integration strategy, not a guarantee of automatic non-blocking behavior.

System qualities

The Reactive Manifesto

The chapter describes responsive, resilient, elastic and message-driven systems. These are design goals, not automatic consequences of using a particular library.

Execution model

Short handlers

Event loops coordinate many connections; they depend on handlers returning promptly and on backpressure and resource limits.

03

Compose asynchronous work

Callback-based APIs return control before a result is ready, but nested callbacks can become hard to follow. CompletableFuture represents one eventual result; thenCompose chains dependent asynchronous operations. It does not itself turn blocking I/O into non-blocking I/O.

AsyncChatDemo.javaJDK 21+
import java.util.Locale;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;

public class AsyncChatDemo {
    static CompletableFuture<String> chat(String input, ExecutorService executor) {
        return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(
            () -> "Echo: " + input.toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT), executor);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            chat("hello", executor)
                .thenCompose(reply -> chat(reply, executor))
                .thenAccept(System.out::println)
                .join(); // wait at the application boundary
        }
    }
}

Runnable JDK 21+ example adapted from the chapter’s chat example. Save as AsyncChatDemo.java; run javac AsyncChatDemo.java and java AsyncChatDemo. It simulates a response and waits at the boundary; it does not contact a service.

04

From one result to a stream

Reactive streams model sequences of items and terminal signals. A Publisher provides items, a Subscriber consumes them, a Subscription manages demand and cancellation, and a Processor can be both subscriber and publisher. A stream can complete successfully or terminate with an error.

Project Reactor’s Flux represents zero to many items and Mono zero or one. Operators such as filter and map describe transformations; in this cold Flux.just example, subscription starts delivery. Not every source is cold or asynchronous, and adding operators does not automatically change threads.

ReactorPipelineDemo.javaJDK 17+ · Reactor
import reactor.core.publisher.Flux;

public class ReactorPipelineDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Flux.just(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
            .filter(n -> n % 2 == 0)
            .map(n -> "Value: " + n)
            .subscribe(System.out::println,
                       error -> System.err.println("Error: " + error),
                       () -> System.out.println("Done!"));
    }
}

Adapted from the chapter’s Reactor example. Expected output: Value: 2, Value: 4, then Done!. It requires the external Reactor library; the HTML itself remains offline.

Dependency and run instructions for this Reactor example

Create a Maven project, save the following as pom.xml and the Java example as src/main/java/ReactorPipelineDemo.java. With JDK 17+ and Maven installed, run mvn compile exec:java -Dexec.mainClass=ReactorPipelineDemo. Maven must download the dependencies and plugins; use a version suitable for your project.

pom.xmlMaven
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0
             https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
  <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>
  <groupId>example</groupId>

  <version>1.0</version>

    <maven.compiler.release>17</maven.compiler.release>
    <project.build.sourceEncoding>UTF-8</project.build.sourceEncoding>
  </properties>

    <dependency>
      <groupId>io.projectreactor</groupId>

    </plugin>
  </plugins></build>
