Reactive streams differ from java.util.stream.Stream: the latter is primarily a pull-oriented computation abstraction, while Reactive Streams defines a subscription protocol with asynchronous demand management. Java Streams can also process non-collection sources or run in parallel; neither API automatically makes underlying work non-blocking.

05

Backpressure is demand

Backpressure lets a subscriber signal how many items it is ready to receive through request(n). It helps coordinate production and consumption, but the entire system must still choose how to handle a source that cannot be slowed.

StrategyTrade-off
Bounded bufferAbsorbs a burst, but needs an explicit overflow policy; an unbounded buffer can exhaust memory.
Drop / sampleReduces load by discarding data; only appropriate when missed events are acceptable.
LatestKeeps the most recent update; intermediate values can be lost.
ErrorFails on overflow so callers can detect and handle overload.

The book illustrates these with price feeds and Reactor operators. The following dependency-free Java Flow example requests items one at a time; Flow provides interfaces corresponding to the Reactive Streams model.

DemandDemo.javaJDK 10+
import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;
import java.util.concurrent.Flow;
import java.util.concurrent.SubmissionPublisher;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;

public class DemandDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        CountDownLatch done = new CountDownLatch(1);
        try (var publisher = new SubmissionPublisher<Integer>()) {
            publisher.subscribe(new Flow.Subscriber<Integer>() {
                private Flow.Subscription subscription;
                public void onSubscribe(Flow.Subscription s) {
                    subscription = s;
                    s.request(1); // request one item initially
                }
                public void onNext(Integer item) {
                    System.out.println("Received " + item);
                    subscription.request(1); // ask for the next item
                }
                public void onError(Throwable error) {
                    error.printStackTrace();
                    done.countDown();
                }
                public void onComplete() {
                    System.out.println("Done");
                    done.countDown();
                }
            });
            for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) publisher.submit(i);
            publisher.close(); // deliver completion after queued items
            if (!done.await(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("Subscriber did not finish");
            }
        }
    }
}

Runnable JDK 10+ example; save as DemandDemo.java. The subscriber asks for one item at a time and waits for completion. SubmissionPublisher.submit() can block when its buffer is full; this is not a demonstration of a fully non-blocking producer.

06

Where virtual threads fit

The chapter compares a reactive price feed with imperative virtual-thread processing. Virtual threads make it practical to express many waiting operations with ordinary blocking code, but they do not automatically provide stream operators, demand signaling, bounded queues or ordering guarantees.

A bounded blocking queue can apply backpressure to a producer: put() waits when capacity is full and take() waits when it is empty. This bounds queued items and provides local flow control, not a time-based rate limit or a bound on all concurrent work.

BoundedQueueDemo.javaJDK 21+
import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;

public class BoundedQueueDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        var queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<Integer>(2);
        try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            var producer = executor.submit(() -> {
                for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) queue.put(i);
                return null;
            });
            var consumer = executor.submit(() -> {
                for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
                    System.out.println("Processed " + queue.take());
                }
                return null;
            });
            producer.get();
            consumer.get();
        }
    }
}

Runnable JDK 21+ example; save as BoundedQueueDemo.java. The finite demo waits for both tasks and uses a capacity of two. Real applications also need shutdown, failure, interruption and timeout policies.

Book example caveat: an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue does not impose a useful fixed capacity by default, and closing an executor waits for submitted tasks. Long-running producer/consumer loops need an explicit stop or cancellation protocol before closure.
07

Pick for the workload

ApproachStrengthsCosts / limits
Reactive streamsComposes asynchronous event sequences, transformations and demand policies.Requires stream expertise, careful scheduler choices, debugging and error handling.
Virtual threadsFamiliar imperative style for many concurrently waiting tasks.Resource limits, cancellation, ordering and flow control remain application concerns.

Both can be useful in the same application; neither is automatically faster or simpler for every team. CPU-bound work remains constrained by available compute, and reactive code can still involve shared state or blocking operators. Match the model to the data flow, libraries and team skills, then measure under representative load.

08

Keep these ideas

  • Readiness-based I/O and virtual-thread blocking solve waiting differently. Neither eliminates protocol or resource constraints.
  • Keep event-loop handlers short; deliberately offload blocking work.
  • CompletableFuture composes individual results; reactive streams model sequences and demand.
  • Backpressure requires an explicit overload policy. Buffer, drop, sample, retain latest or fail according to the application.
  • Virtual threads and reactive pipelines can coexist. Choose and measure rather than treating one as a universal replacement.

Source: A N M Bazlur Rahman, Modern Concurrency in Java, 1st ed., O’Reilly Media, 2025, Chapter 6, “The Relevance of Reactive Java in Light of Virtual Threads,” pp. 247–295 (PDF pages 265–313). Figures 6-1 and 6-2 are embedded from the supplied PDF. Copyright © 2025 A N M Bazlur Rahman. Explanations and code examples are adapted for study.

Chapter 07 · Modern frameworks utilizing virtual threads

Frameworks offer different ways to run supported work on virtual threads: configuration in Spring Boot, targeted annotations in Quarkus, and managed concurrency in Jakarta EE.

01

Spring Boot: configuration first

Spring Boot 3.2 introduced a virtual-thread configuration option. On a supported JDK 21+ application, it can configure eligible infrastructure such as task execution, scheduling and supported embedded-server request handling. Actual behavior depends on the Boot version, server, execution path and any user-supplied beans; the setting does not make every application thread virtual.

application.propertiesSpring Boot · JDK 21+
# src/main/resources/application.properties
spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true
# Useful when the application depends on scheduled/async work to stay alive:
spring.main.keep-alive=true

Configuration for a compatible Spring Boot project. Virtual threads are daemon threads; spring.main.keep-alive can keep an application relying on scheduled or asynchronous work alive.

A Spring MVC controller can check the actual thread handling a request:

GreetingController.javaSpring MVC
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

@RestController
public class GreetingController {
    @GetMapping("/hello")
    public String hello() {
        Thread thread = Thread.currentThread();
        return "Hello! Virtual thread: " + thread.isVirtual();
    }
}

Framework example adapted from the chapter. Add this class to an existing Spring Boot MVC application using spring-boot-starter-web, JDK 21+, and the property above. Run the application and request /hello; the result depends on the embedded server and configuration. This is not a standalone Java file.

The chapter also shows Callable-returning MVC methods, @Async methods and scheduled tasks. Each uses framework-managed execution; verify the actual executor or scheduler rather than assuming the request setting applies everywhere. Virtual threads do not remove downstream connection limits or make CPU-bound tasks faster.

02

Custom Spring executors

When a project needs explicit control, Spring can adapt a JDK virtual-thread executor. The following example registers the underlying executor as its own bean so Spring can close it; the adapter supplies the framework’s AsyncTaskExecutor interface.

VirtualExecutorConfig.javaSpring Boot
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.core.task.AsyncTaskExecutor;
import org.springframework.core.task.support.TaskExecutorAdapter;
import org.springframework.scheduling.annotation.EnableAsync;

@Configuration
@EnableAsync
public class VirtualExecutorConfig {
    @Bean(destroyMethod = "close")
    ExecutorService virtualExecutor() {
        return Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor();
    }

    @Bean(name = "applicationTaskExecutor")
    AsyncTaskExecutor applicationTaskExecutor(ExecutorService virtualExecutor) {
        return new TaskExecutorAdapter(virtualExecutor);
    }
}
GreetingService.javaSpring @Async
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import org.springframework.scheduling.annotation.Async;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@Service
public class GreetingService {
    @Async("applicationTaskExecutor")
    public CompletableFuture<String> greeting() {
        return CompletableFuture.completedFuture(
            "Virtual: " + Thread.currentThread().isVirtual());
    }
}

Two framework classes for a Spring Boot project on JDK 21+ with compatible Spring Framework APIs. Invoke the @Async method through a Spring-managed proxy from another bean; self-invocation does not normally activate proxy-based asynchronous execution.

Lifecycle and scope: this custom bean configures the named application task executor, not every server or scheduler. Custom executors can change or replace auto-configuration; review the framework’s bean-selection rules and shut down owned resources.
03

Quarkus: targeted dispatch

Quarkus integrates with Vert.x and can offload supported endpoint work to a virtual thread with @RunOnVirtualThread. This preserves the event loop for short non-blocking handlers while letting selected operations use imperative blocking-style code.

GreetingResource.javaQuarkus REST
import io.smallrye.common.annotation.RunOnVirtualThread;
import jakarta.ws.rs.GET;
import jakarta.ws.rs.Path;
import jakarta.ws.rs.Produces;
import jakarta.ws.rs.core.MediaType;

@Path("/hello")
public class GreetingResource {
    @GET
    @RunOnVirtualThread
    @Produces(MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN)
    public String hello() {
        return "Hello! Virtual thread: " + Thread.currentThread().isVirtual();
    }
}

Framework example for an existing Quarkus REST application with the quarkus-rest extension and JDK 21+. Add it as a resource class and request /hello. In Quarkus REST, the annotation applies to endpoints considered blocking, including this String-returning example; check your version and extensions.

The chapter also illustrates a MicroProfile REST client and a Mutiny Uni awaited with a timeout from a virtual-thread endpoint. Such integration needs the appropriate client extension and configuration. Waiting from a virtual thread can be appropriate; blocking an event-loop thread remains harmful.

04

Jakarta EE: managed concurrency

Jakarta Concurrency 3.1 adds virtual = true to managed executor, scheduled-executor and thread-factory definitions. These resources remain managed by the application server, which can provide its concurrency and context-management rules.

GreetingEndpoint.javaJakarta EE
import jakarta.annotation.Resource;
import jakarta.enterprise.concurrent.ManagedExecutorDefinition;
import jakarta.enterprise.concurrent.ManagedExecutorService;
import jakarta.ws.rs.GET;
import jakarta.ws.rs.Path;
import jakarta.ws.rs.Produces;
import jakarta.ws.rs.core.MediaType;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException;

@ManagedExecutorDefinition(
    name = "java:module/concurrent/virtualExecutor", virtual = true)
@Path("/hello")
public class GreetingEndpoint {
    @Resource(lookup = "java:module/concurrent/virtualExecutor")
    ManagedExecutorService executor;

    @GET
    @Produces(MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN)
    public String hello() throws InterruptedException, ExecutionException {
        return executor.submit(() ->
            "Managed task virtual: " + Thread.currentThread().isVirtual()).get();
    }
}

Framework example for a compatible Jakarta EE runtime implementing Jakarta Concurrency 3.1 and JAX-RS. The deployment’s JAX-RS application path determines the full URL. get() waits on the calling request thread; only the submitted task’s thread is being checked.

virtual = true requests virtual-thread support; the runtime, Java version and vendor configuration determine whether it is available. Check the target server’s documentation rather than assuming every task is virtual or relying on an implicit fallback. Scheduled executors and managed thread factories have corresponding definition annotations.

05

Try a JDK-only example

The book uses the JDK’s lightweight HttpServer as a simulated remote service. This adapted demo starts a loopback server on a temporary port, handles one request with a virtual-thread executor, prints the response and shuts down. It is an educational local example, not a production server.

VirtualHttpDemo.javaJDK 21+
import com.sun.net.httpserver.HttpServer;
import java.net.InetSocketAddress;
import java.net.URI;
import java.net.http.HttpClient;
import java.net.http.HttpRequest;
import java.net.http.HttpResponse;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;

public class VirtualHttpDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        var server = HttpServer.create(new InetSocketAddress("127.0.0.1", 0), 0);
        try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            server.setExecutor(executor);
            server.createContext("/hello", exchange -> {
                byte[] body = ("Virtual handler: " + Thread.currentThread().isVirtual())
                    .getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
                exchange.getResponseHeaders().set("Content-Type", "text/plain; charset=utf-8");
                exchange.sendResponseHeaders(200, body.length);
                try (var output = exchange.getResponseBody()) {
                    output.write(body);
                }
            });
            server.start();
            try {
                var client = HttpClient.newBuilder()
                    .connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(3)).build();
                var request = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
                    .uri(URI.create("http://127.0.0.1:" + server.getAddress().getPort() + "/hello"))
                    .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(3)).build();
                System.out.println(client.send(request, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()).body());
            } finally {
                server.stop(0);
            }
        }
    }
}
Compile & runShell
# JDK 21+; the server starts on an ephemeral loopback port and stops itself.
javac --add-modules jdk.httpserver VirtualHttpDemo.java
java --add-modules jdk.httpserver VirtualHttpDemo

Complete JDK 21+ example; save as VirtualHttpDemo.java. It uses the JDK’s jdk.httpserver and java.net.http modules, not Spring, Quarkus or Jakarta EE. Expected output: Virtual handler: true.

06

Adoption checklist

  • Confirm the execution path. Log or inspect Thread.currentThread().isVirtual() for the work you actually care about.
  • Choose the integration deliberately. Framework auto-configuration, custom executors and managed resources have different scopes and lifecycles.
  • Protect scarce resources. Bound database connections, remote calls and queues; virtual threads do not make them unlimited.
  • Review library compatibility and context propagation. Check thread-local usage, blocking behavior, cancellation and pinning for your JDK version.
  • Measure under realistic load. Watch throughput, latency, CPU, memory, JFR events and downstream saturation before and after the change.

The chapter also mentions Helidon and Micronaut. Their virtual-thread support is version- and configuration-dependent; consult the specific framework and server documentation rather than assuming all requests automatically use virtual threads.

Source: A N M Bazlur Rahman, Modern Concurrency in Java, 1st ed., O’Reilly Media, 2025, Chapter 7, “Modern Frameworks Utilizing Virtual Threads,” pp. 297–309 (PDF pages 315–327). The chapter contains no numbered figures; the study diagram above is an original illustration. Explanations and code examples are adapted for study.

Chapter 08 · Conclusion and takeaways

Choose the concurrency model for the workload, introduce changes gradually, and use observation—not assumptions—to guide the next step.

01

Choose the right model

The book closes by contrasting three approaches. Virtual threads make a familiar thread-per-task style practical for many concurrent operations that spend time waiting. Platform-thread pools remain useful for bounded CPU-intensive work and some legacy or native integrations. Reactive streams are useful for event flows, transformations and explicit demand management.

ApproachGood starting pointRemember
Virtual threadsMany concurrent, waiting-heavy tasks.Not every blocking operation releases its carrier; resource limits still apply.
Platform-thread poolsControlled worker concurrency, including CPU-bound processing.Size and queue policy need measurement; more threads cannot create more CPU capacity.
Reactive streamsOngoing event streams and demand-aware processing.Backpressure, scheduler choices and operator behavior require explicit design.

These approaches can coexist. Virtual threads primarily improve scalability for appropriate waiting-heavy workloads; they are not a promise of lower latency or a universal replacement for other models.

02

Make migration incremental

Rather than switching an entire legacy system overnight, start with a small, independent I/O-heavy service or operation. Establish a baseline, review dependencies, deploy gradually and compare outcomes. Keep a rollback path, share what the team learns, and expand only after the results justify it.

Structured concurrency can help give related tasks a clear lifetime, while scoped values can carry bounded context. Their exact API availability depends on the JDK: ScopedValue is final in JDK 25, while the StructuredTaskScope API shown in Chapter 4 is a JDK 25 preview.

03

Keep resources bounded

Virtual threads are inexpensive compared with platform threads, but databases, services, memory and CPU remain finite. The following original example illustrates the book’s migration principle: use virtual threads for tasks while explicitly limiting access to a simulated scarce resource.

MigrationExample.javaJDK 21+
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.Future;
import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException;

public class MigrationExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        var resourceSlots = new Semaphore(2);
        try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            var tasks = new ArrayList<Future<String>>();
            for (int i = 1; i <= 4; i++) {
                final int id = i;
                tasks.add(executor.submit(() -> {
                    if (!resourceSlots.tryAcquire(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {
                        throw new TimeoutException("Resource busy");
                    }
                    try {
                        Thread.sleep(50); // simulate waiting for a service
                        return "Task " + id + " completed";
                    } finally {
                        resourceSlots.release();
                    }
                }));
            }
            for (Future<String> task : tasks) {
                System.out.println(task.get());
            }
        } // waits for submitted tasks and closes the executor
    }
}
Compile & runShell
# Requires JDK 21 or newer.
javac MigrationExample.java
java MigrationExample

Runnable JDK 21+ illustration, not an example from Chapter 8. Save as MigrationExample.java. The semaphore allows at most two tasks into the protected section; the timeout applies to acquiring a permit, not the entire task. The sleep simulates waiting, not a real database call or benchmark.

04

Monitor & learn

Measure request latency and throughput along with CPU, heap, garbage collection, queue depth, connection usage and downstream saturation. Use Java Flight Recorder and virtual-thread-aware diagnostics to investigate contention and pinning.

Pinning

Check the JDK

In JDK 21–23, blocking inside synchronized can pin a carrier. JDK 24 greatly reduces monitor-related pinning; native interactions and other cases can still matter.

Context

Audit ThreadLocal

Per-thread state may consume significant memory across many virtual threads. Review initialization, lifetime, inheritance and cleanup.

Use realistic load tests and update your practices as the JDK and framework ecosystem evolve. The book emphasizes team education, continuous learning and feedback alongside the technical changes.

05

Final takeaways

  • Match the model to the work: waiting-heavy tasks, CPU-intensive computation and event streams have different needs.
  • Adopt gradually and measure. Keep a baseline and validate latency, throughput and resource use.
  • Protect shared resources and handle cancellation. Lightweight threads do not remove capacity limits.
  • Watch pinning and thread-local state using diagnostics appropriate to your JDK and workload.
  • Keep learning. Java’s concurrency APIs, frameworks and operational guidance continue to evolve.

Source: A N M Bazlur Rahman, Modern Concurrency in Java, 1st ed., O’Reilly Media, 2025, Chapter 8, “Conclusion and Takeaways,” pp. 311–312 (PDF pages 329–330). The chapter contains no numbered figures or code examples; the study diagram and Java illustration above are original.
